items.stem: What is the relative mass of an electron, compared with a proton of relative mass 1?
items.markingKey: Electron relative mass ≈ 1/1836 (negligible); proton 1; neutron 1.

items.stem: Explain why a beam of electrons is deflected through a much larger angle than a beam of protons in the same electric field.
items.answer: The charges are equal in size, but an electron has about 1/1836 of the mass of a proton, so its charge-to-mass ratio is much larger and it is deflected more.
items.markingKey: same size charge; much smaller mass / larger charge-to-mass ratio [2]

items.stem: Explain why protons and electrons are deflected in opposite directions between charged plates.
items.answer: They have opposite charges: protons (+) are attracted to the negative plate and electrons (−) to the positive plate.
items.markingKey: opposite charges; attraction to oppositely charged plate [2]

items.stem: A beam of ¹H⁺ ions is deflected through an angle of 12° when it passes between two charged plates. Calculate the angle through which a beam of ³H⁺ ions, travelling at the same speed, would be deflected by the same plates.
items.markingKey: angle ∝ charge/mass [1]; ¹H⁺ ions: 1/1, ³H⁺ ions: 1/3 [1]; angle = 12 × (1/3) ÷ (1/1) = 4.00° [1]

items.stem: A beam of ⁴He⁺ ions is deflected through an angle of 2° when it passes between two charged plates. Calculate the angle through which a beam of ⁶Li³⁺ ions, travelling at the same speed, would be deflected by the same plates.
items.markingKey: angle ∝ charge/mass [1]; ⁴He⁺ ions: 1/4, ⁶Li³⁺ ions: 3/6 [1]; angle = 2 × (3/6) ÷ (1/4) = 4.00° [1]

items.stem: A physics–chemistry project in Dubai studies how ions and sub-atomic particles move in an electric field. (a) Copy and complete a table giving the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron. (b) Suggest why a beam of ²H⁺ ions could be used to distinguish deuterium from ¹H⁺.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) ²H⁺ has twice the mass and the same charge, so it is deflected through half the angle.
items.markingKey: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 [2] (b) ²H⁺ has twice the mass and the same charge, so it is deflected through half the angle. [2]

items.stem: Explain why an atom is electrically neutral even though it contains charged particles.
items.answer: It contains equal numbers of protons (+1) and electrons (−1), so the charges cancel; neutrons are uncharged.
items.markingKey: equal numbers of p and e; charges cancel [2]

items.stem: Suggest why ²H⁺ ions are deflected less than ¹H⁺ ions in the same electric field.
items.answer: Both have charge +1 but ²H⁺ has twice the mass, so its charge-to-mass ratio is halved and it is deflected less (about half the angle).
items.markingKey: same charge; greater mass so smaller charge/mass ratio [2]

items.stem: Which beam is deflected most in an electric field: ²H⁺ ions or ⁶Li⁺ ions?
items.answer: ²H⁺ ions
items.markingKey: Deflection ∝ charge/mass: ²H⁺ ions 0.500, ⁶Li⁺ ions 0.167.

items.stem: A beam of ²H⁺ ions is deflected through an angle of 6° when it passes between two charged plates. Calculate the angle through which a beam of ⁶Li⁺ ions, travelling at the same speed, would be deflected by the same plates.
items.markingKey: angle ∝ charge/mass [1]; ²H⁺ ions: 1/2, ⁶Li⁺ ions: 1/6 [1]; angle = 6 × (1/6) ÷ (1/2) = 2.00° [1]

items.stem: In a research laboratory, beams of different particles are fired between two charged plates and the angles of deflection are measured. (a) A beam of ²H⁺ ions is deflected by 4°. Calculate the angle of deflection of ¹H⁺ ions under the same conditions. (b) Suggest why a beam of ²H⁺ ions could be used to distinguish deuterium from ¹H⁺.
items.answer: (a) 8.00° (b) ²H⁺ has twice the mass and the same charge, so it is deflected through half the angle.
items.markingKey: (a) angle ∝ charge/mass; 4 × 1.00/0.500 = 8.00° [2] (b) ²H⁺ has twice the mass and the same charge, so it is deflected through half the angle. [2]

items.stem: What are isotopes?
options: atoms with the same nucleon number but different proton numbers
ions of the same element with different charges
atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
atoms of different elements with the same number of neutrons
items.answer: atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
items.markingKey: Isotopes: same proton (atomic) number, different neutron number, so different nucleon (mass) number.

items.stem: Explain why atomic radius decreases across Period 3.
items.answer: Nuclear charge (number of protons) increases while shielding stays roughly the same (same number of inner shells), so the outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.
items.markingKey: increasing nuclear charge; similar shielding / same shell [2]

items.stem: Explain why atomic radius increases down a group.
items.answer: Each element has an extra occupied shell, so the outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded, outweighing the increased nuclear charge.
items.markingKey: extra shell/further away; more shielding [2]

items.stem: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom ⁷Li.
items.answer: 3 protons, 4 neutrons, 3 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 3 [1]; neutrons = A − Z = 7 − 3 = 4 [1]; electrons = 3 [1]

items.stem: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the atom ²³Na.
items.answer: 11 protons, 12 neutrons, 11 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 11 [1]; neutrons = A − Z = 23 − 11 = 12 [1]; electrons = 11 [1]

items.stem: Sipho is researching the isotopes of magnesium, ²⁴Mg and ²⁶Mg, for a project in Kuala Lumpur. (a) Explain why the two isotopes have the same chemical properties. (b) State how the atomic radius of magnesium compares with that of the element directly above it in the Periodic Table, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) Same number of electrons / same electronic configuration; chemical reactions involve electrons. (b) Larger: one more occupied shell, outer electrons further from the nucleus and more shielded.
items.markingKey: (a) Same number of electrons / same electronic configuration; chemical reactions involve electrons. [2] (b) Larger: one more occupied shell, outer electrons further from the nucleus and more shielded. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a sodium ion, Na⁺, is much smaller than a sodium atom.
items.answer: Na⁺ has lost its outer (3s) shell, so it has one fewer shell; also the 11 protons now attract only 10 electrons, so they are held closer.
items.markingKey: one fewer shell; same nuclear charge on fewer electrons [2]

items.stem: Explain why a chloride ion, Cl⁻, is larger than a chlorine atom.
items.answer: Cl⁻ has an extra electron in the same outer shell; increased repulsion between electrons and the same nuclear charge (17 protons for 18 electrons) means the electron cloud expands.
items.markingKey: extra electron, more repulsion; same nuclear charge [2]

items.stem: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion ³⁴S²⁻.
items.answer: 16 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 16 [1]; neutrons = A − Z = 34 − 16 = 18 [1]; electrons = 16 − (-2) = 18 [1]

items.stem: A species X has 26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons. Use the Periodic Table to identify X and write its full symbol, showing nucleon number, proton number and charge.
items.answer: iron: ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ (proton number 26)
items.markingKey: Z = 26 identifies iron [1]; A = 26 + 30 = 56 [1]; charge = 26 − 23 = +3 [1]; correct symbol ⁵⁶Fe³⁺ [1]

items.stem: Arjun is researching the isotopes of bromine, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, for a project in Nairobi. (a) Define the term isotopes. (b) State one physical property that differs between the isotopes. (c) Compare the radius of the Br⁻ ion with that of the bromine atom, and explain.
items.answer: (a) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. (b) Density / mass / rate of diffusion (of the element or its compounds). (c) The ion is larger: extra electron(s) increase repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. [1] (b) Density / mass / rate of diffusion (of the element or its compounds). [1] (c) The ion is larger: extra electron(s) increase repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged. [2]

items.stem: Relative atomic mass is defined relative to which standard?
options: one-sixteenth of the mass of an oxygen-16 atom
one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
the mass of one hydrogen atom
items.answer: one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
items.markingKey: Ar = weighted mean mass of an atom ÷ (1/12 × mass of one ¹²C atom).

items.stem: Explain why the relative atomic mass of chlorine, 35.5, is not a whole number.
items.answer: Chlorine is a mixture of isotopes (³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl); Ar is a weighted mean of their masses based on abundance.
items.markingKey: mixture of isotopes; weighted mean [2]

items.stem: Explain why the Cl₂ molecular-ion peaks at m/e 70, 72 and 74 have heights in the ratio 9 : 6 : 1.
items.answer: Probabilities with ³⁵Cl : ³⁷Cl = 3 : 1: ³⁵Cl–³⁵Cl = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; ³⁵Cl–³⁷Cl (two ways) = 2 × 3/4 × 1/4 = 6/16; ³⁷Cl–³⁷Cl = 1/16.
items.markingKey: identifies isotope combinations [1]; probabilities give 9 : 6 : 1 [1]

items.stem: Naturally occurring silicon has the isotopic composition ²⁸Si 92.2%, ²⁹Si 4.7%, ³⁰Si 3.1%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon to three significant figures.
Naturally occurring copper has the isotopic composition ⁶³Cu 69.2%, ⁶⁵Cu 30.8%. Calculate the relative atomic mass of copper to three significant figures.

Hana records the mass spectrum of a sample of lithium in a school laboratory. Peaks: m/e 6 (7.5%), m/e 7 (92.5%). (a) State what is plotted on each axis of a mass spectrum. (b) Explain why each peak is due to a different isotope rather than a different element. (c) Suggest why a small peak may appear at half of one of the m/e values. (d) Calculate the relative formula mass of the chloride LiCl, using Ar(Cl) = 35.5 and your answer above.
items.answer: (a) x-axis: mass-to-charge ratio (m/e); y-axis: relative abundance (intensity). (b) All peaks come from atoms of the same element (same proton number) that differ only in neutron number and so in mass. (c) A doubly charged ion (2+) of that isotope has m/e equal to half its mass. (d) 42.4
items.markingKey: (a) x-axis: mass-to-charge ratio (m/e); y-axis: relative abundance (intensity). [1] (b) All peaks come from atoms of the same element (same proton number) that differ only in neutron number and so in mass. [1] (c) A doubly charged ion (2+) of that isotope has m/e equal to half its mass. [1] (d) 42.4 [1]

items.stem: Explain why Br₂ gives three molecular-ion peaks at m/e 158, 160 and 162 in a ratio of about 1 : 2 : 1.
items.answer: ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br are present in roughly equal amounts; ⁷⁹Br⁷⁹Br, ⁷⁹Br⁸¹Br (two ways) and ⁸¹Br⁸¹Br give 1 : 2 : 1.
items.markingKey: about 1 : 1 isotopes [1]; mixed molecule can form two ways [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass.
items.answer: Relative isotopic mass is for one isotope; relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of the isotopic masses of all naturally occurring isotopes, both relative to 1/12 of ¹²C.
items.markingKey: isotopic = single isotope [1]; Ar = weighted mean [1]

items.stem: A sample of gallium from a geological survey in Bangkok contains only ⁶⁹Ga and ⁷¹Ga. Its relative atomic mass is 69.75. Calculate the percentage abundance of ⁶⁹Ga.

Hana records the mass spectrum of a sample of gallium in an AS practical class. Peaks: m/e 69 (60.1%), m/e 71 (39.9%). (a) Define relative atomic mass. (b) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the element to three significant figures. (c) State what is plotted on each axis of a mass spectrum. (d) Suggest why a small peak may appear at half of one of the m/e values.
items.answer: (a) The weighted mean mass of an atom of the element relative to 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. (b) 69.8 (c) x-axis: mass-to-charge ratio (m/e); y-axis: relative abundance (intensity). (d) A doubly charged ion (2+) of that isotope has m/e equal to half its mass.
items.markingKey: (a) The weighted mean mass of an atom of the element relative to 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. [2] (b) Σ(m × %)/100 = 69.8 [2] (c) x-axis: mass-to-charge ratio (m/e); y-axis: relative abundance (intensity). [1] (d) A doubly charged ion (2+) of that isotope has m/e equal to half its mass. [1]

items.stem: What is the Avogadro constant?
options: the number of atoms in 1 g of hydrogen
the volume of one mole of gas at r.t.p.
the number of particles in one mole of a substance, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
the mass of one mole of a substance
items.answer: the number of particles in one mole of a substance, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹: the number of atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.

items.stem: Explain why the empirical formula and molecular formula of propanone, C₃H₆O, are the same.
items.answer: The numbers of atoms 3 : 6 : 1 have no common factor, so the simplest ratio is the molecular formula itself.
items.markingKey: no common factor [1]; simplest ratio equals actual numbers [1]

items.stem: Explain why 1 mol of hydrogen gas and 1 mol of helium gas contain different numbers of atoms.
items.answer: Both contain 6.02 × 10²³ particles, but hydrogen exists as H₂ molecules (2 atoms each) whereas helium is monatomic, so H₂ has 1.20 × 10²⁴ atoms.
items.markingKey: same number of particles [1]; H₂ diatomic so twice the atoms [1]

items.stem: A compound has the composition by mass C 80.0%, H 20.0%. Calculate its empirical formula.
items.answer: CH₃
items.markingKey: divide % by Ar [1]; divide by smallest and round to whole numbers: CH₃ [1]

items.stem: Compound Y, used in a dye works in Lisbon, has the composition by mass C 54.5%, H 9.1%, O 36.4%. Its relative molecular mass is 88.0. Calculate the empirical formula and the molecular formula of Y.
items.answer: empirical C₂H₄O; molecular C₄H₈O₂
items.markingKey: moles: % ÷ Ar [1]; ratio → C₂H₄O [1]; Mr(empirical) = 44.0 [1]; 88.0/44.0 = 2 so C₄H₈O₂ [1]

items.stem: Compound Y, used in a university project in Auckland, has the composition by mass H 12.5%, N 87.5%. Its relative molecular mass is 32.0. Calculate the empirical formula and the molecular formula of Y.
items.answer: empirical H₂N; molecular N₂H₄
items.markingKey: moles: % ÷ Ar [1]; ratio → H₂N [1]; Mr(empirical) = 16.0 [1]; 32.0/16.0 = 2 so N₂H₄ [1]

items.stem: An environmental chemist in Istanbul isolates a pollutant with composition H 5.9%, O 94.1%. Mass spectrometry shows Mr = 34.0. (a) Calculate the empirical formula. (b) Calculate the number of molecules in 1.5 g of the compound. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
items.markingKey: (a) divide by Ar, then by smallest, whole-number ratio [2] (b) n = 1.5/34.0; × L [2]

items.stem: Sofia analyses an unknown liquid in a research laboratory. It has the composition by mass C 24.2%, H 4.0%, Cl 71.7% and Mr = 99.0. (a) Define the term empirical formula. (b) Calculate the empirical formula. (c) Deduce the molecular formula, showing your working.
items.answer: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. (b) CH₂Cl (c) C₂H₄Cl₂
items.markingKey: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. [1] (b) divide by Ar, then by smallest, whole-number ratio [2] (c) Mr(empirical) = 49.5; 99.0/49.5 = 2 [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the empirical formula of a compound?
options: the formula of one mole of the compound
the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in the compound
the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule
the formula showing how atoms are bonded
items.answer: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in the compound
items.markingKey: Molecular formula = actual numbers of atoms in a molecule; empirical = simplest ratio.

items.stem: Which compound has the same empirical formula as ethanoic acid, C₂H₄O₂?
items.answer: glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆
items.markingKey: Both reduce to CH₂O.

items.stem: Explain why the empirical formula alone is not enough to identify a molecular compound.
items.answer: Many compounds share an empirical formula (e.g. CH₂O for methanal, ethanoic acid and glucose); Mr is needed to find the molecular formula.
items.markingKey: several compounds share it [1]; need Mr [1]

items.stem: Priya, a student in Muscat, heats 8.05 g of hydrated sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄·xH₂O, to constant mass. The anhydrous residue has a mass of 3.55 g. Calculate the value of x.
items.markingKey: mass of water = 4.50 g; n(H₂O) = 0.250 mol [1]; n(Na₂SO₄) = 3.55/142.1 = 0.0250 mol [1]; ratio = 10 [1]

items.stem: Mateo, a student in Cape Town, heats 12.9 g of hydrated sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄·xH₂O, to constant mass. The anhydrous residue has a mass of 5.68 g. Calculate the value of x.
items.markingKey: mass of water = 7.20 g; n(H₂O) = 0.400 mol [1]; n(Na₂SO₄) = 5.68/142.1 = 0.0400 mol [1]; ratio = 10 [1]

items.stem: Priya analyses an unknown liquid in an AS practical class. It has the composition by mass C 84.2%, H 15.8% and Mr = 114.0. (a) Calculate the empirical formula. (b) Deduce the molecular formula, showing your working. (c) Calculate the number of molecules in 3.0 g of the compound. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
items.answer: (a) C₄H₉ (b) C₈H₁₈ (c) 1.58 × 10²²
items.markingKey: (a) divide by Ar, then by smallest, whole-number ratio [2] (b) Mr(empirical) = 57.0; 114.0/57.0 = 2 [2] (c) n = 3.0/114.0; × L [2]

items.stem: What volume does one mole of any gas occupy at room temperature and pressure?
items.answer: 24.0 dm³
items.markingKey: Molar gas volume at r.t.p. = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ (24 000 cm³).

items.stem: Explain why the burette is rinsed with the solution it will contain rather than with water.
items.answer: Water left in the burette would dilute the solution and change its concentration, making the titre too large.
items.markingKey: water dilutes [1]; effect on titre [1]

items.stem: Explain the term limiting reagent.
items.answer: The reactant that is completely used up first; it determines the maximum amount of product, the other reactant being in excess.
items.markingKey: used up first [1]; determines amount of product [1]

items.stem: Calculate the mass of H₂ formed when 1.20 g of Na reacts completely: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
For the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, calculate the volume of H₂ at room temperature and pressure formed from 12.0 g of Mg reacting completely.
items.answer: 11.9 dm³

items.stem: Calculate the mass of CO₂ formed when 15.0 g of O₂ reacts completely: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. In practice 11.0 g was obtained. Calculate the percentage yield.

A water-treatment works in Seoul checks the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution by titration with 0.150 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid. A 25.0 cm³ sample needs 21.5 cm³ of acid. (a) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. (b) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in mol dm⁻³. (c) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in g dm⁻³.
items.answer: (a) H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (b) 0.258 mol dm⁻³ (c) 10.3 g dm⁻³
items.markingKey: (a) H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O [1] (b) n(alkali) = 0.00645 mol; ÷ 0.0250 [2] (c) × Mr 40.0 [1]

items.stem: A water-treatment works in Muscat checks the concentration of a sodium hydroxide solution by titration with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. A 25.0 cm³ sample needs 24.4 cm³ of acid. (a) Calculate the amount of acid in the mean titre. (b) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in mol dm⁻³. (c) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in g dm⁻³. (d) The burette readings are recorded to the nearest 0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre if each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³.
What is the concentration of a solution containing 0.50 mol of solute in 250 cm³ of solution?
items.answer: 2.0 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State the formula connecting concentration, amount and volume of solution. (b) What is the concentration of a solution containing 0.50 mol of solute in 250 cm³ of solution?
items.answer: (a) c = n/V (V in dm³) (b) 2.0 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Explain why equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.
items.answer: Gas molecules are far apart, so the volume depends on the number of molecules rather than their size (Avogadro’s law).
items.markingKey: molecules far apart/size negligible [1]; volume depends on number [1]

items.stem: For the reaction 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O, what mass of CO₂ is formed from 5.00 g of O₂?
items.markingKey: n ratio 13 : 8; mass = 4.23 g.

items.stem: Ines, a student in Accra, titrates 25.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ potassium hydroxide with sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 23.8 cm³. The equation is H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.0263 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Tomás uses a standard solution of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid to find the concentration of a solution of sodium hydroxide in a research laboratory. 25.0 cm³ of the alkali needed a mean titre of 22.8 cm³. (a) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in mol dm⁻³. (b) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in g dm⁻³.
items.answer: (a) 0.0456 mol dm⁻³ (b) 1.82 g dm⁻³

items.stem: Which particle has a relative charge of 0 and a relative mass of 1?
items.answer: neutron
items.markingKey: Neutron: charge 0, mass 1. Proton: +1, 1. Electron: −1, 1/1836.

items.stem: Describe the structure of an atom in terms of the positions of the sub-atomic particles.
items.answer: A very small, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons is surrounded by electrons in shells (energy levels); most of the atom is empty space.
items.markingKey: nucleus with p and n; electrons in shells around it [2]

items.stem: A beam of ¹H⁺ ions is deflected through an angle of 6° when it passes between two charged plates. Calculate the angle through which a beam of ⁴He²⁺ ions (α-particles), travelling at the same speed, would be deflected by the same plates.
items.markingKey: angle ∝ charge/mass [1]; ¹H⁺ ions: 1/1, ⁴He²⁺ ions (α-particles): 2/4 [1]; angle = 6 × (2/4) ÷ (1/1) = 3.00° [1]

items.stem: In a quality-control laboratory, beams of different particles are fired between two charged plates and the angles of deflection are measured. (a) Copy and complete a table giving the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron. (b) State which beam is not deflected and explain why. (c) Suggest why a beam of ²H⁺ ions could be used to distinguish deuterium from ¹H⁺.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) Neutrons — they have no charge so the electric field exerts no force on them. (c) ²H⁺ has twice the mass and the same charge, so it is deflected through half the angle.
items.markingKey: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 [2] (b) Neutrons — they have no charge so the electric field exerts no force on them. [2] (c) ²H⁺ has twice the mass and the same charge, so it is deflected through half the angle. [2]

items.stem: Why do isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties?
options: They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same electronic configuration
items.answer: They have the same electronic configuration
items.markingKey: Chemistry depends on electrons; isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons.

items.stem: Explain why ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl react in the same way with sodium.
items.answer: Both have 17 protons and 17 electrons with the same electronic configuration; chemical reactions involve electrons, not neutrons.
items.markingKey: same electronic configuration; reactions depend on electrons [2]

items.stem: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion ³⁵Cl⁻.
items.answer: 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 17 [1]; neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18 [1]; electrons = 17 − (-1) = 18 [1]

items.stem: Use the relative atomic masses in the Periodic Table to find the relative formula mass of (NH₄)₂SO₄.
A sample of copper from a geological survey in Lagos contains only ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu. Its relative atomic mass is 63.40. Calculate the percentage abundance of ⁶³Cu.
Bromine consists of ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br in the ratio 1 : 1. Predict the m/e values of the peaks for the molecular ion Br₂⁺ and their relative heights. Explain your answer.
Explain how you would find the formula of a hydrated salt by heating.
items.answer: Weigh, heat to constant mass to remove all water, reweigh; moles of water and anhydrous salt from masses give the ratio x.
items.markingKey: heat to constant mass [1]; calculate mole ratio of water : anhydrous salt [1]

items.stem: A student in Auckland claims that the empirical formula of hexane, C₆H₁₄, is CH₂. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Divide by the highest common factor 2: the empirical formula is C₃H₇.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Calculate the number of molecules (or formula units) in 8.00 g of Pb(NO₃)₂. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
Calculate the total number of atoms in 2.50 g of Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. (L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
items.markingKey: n = 0.00874 mol [1]; × L gives formula units [1]; × 36 atoms per unit = 1.89 × 10²³ [1]

items.stem: An environmental chemist in Toronto isolates a pollutant with composition C 92.3%, H 7.7%. Mass spectrometry shows Mr = 78.0. (a) Define the term empirical formula. (b) Calculate the empirical formula. (c) State the meaning of the term mole.
items.answer: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. (b) CH (c) The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (as many as there are atoms in 12 g of ¹²C).
items.markingKey: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. [1] (b) divide by Ar, then by smallest, whole-number ratio [2] (c) The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (as many as there are atoms in 12 g of ¹²C). [1]

items.stem: Explain why a back titration is used to find the amount of calcium carbonate in an eggshell.
items.answer: CaCO₃ is insoluble and reacts slowly, so a known excess of acid is added and the unreacted acid is titrated with alkali; the acid used = total − excess.
items.markingKey: insoluble/slow so direct titration impractical [1]; excess acid titrated [1]

items.stem: "In a titration calculation, the volume 25.0 cm³ is used directly in c = n/V to give the concentration in mol dm⁻³." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Convert to dm³ first: 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Calculate the mass of CO₂ formed when 6.00 g of CO reacts completely: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

Jonas uses a standard solution of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid to find the concentration of a solution of sodium hydroxide in a college laboratory. 25.0 cm³ of the alkali needed a mean titre of 23.6 cm³. (a) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in mol dm⁻³. (b) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in g dm⁻³. (c) The burette readings are recorded to the nearest 0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre if each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³.

Ana uses a standard solution of 0.0500 mol dm⁻³ sulfuric acid to find the concentration of a solution of sodium hydroxide in an AS practical class. 25.0 cm³ of the alkali needed a mean titre of 23.6 cm³. (a) Calculate the amount of acid in the mean titre. (b) Describe how the titration should be carried out to obtain an accurate mean titre. (c) The burette readings are recorded to the nearest 0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre if each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³.
items.answer: (a) 0.00118 mol (b) Rinse apparatus with the solutions; pipette 25.0 cm³ alkali into a conical flask with indicator; add acid from the burette, swirling, dropwise near the end-point; repeat to concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³). (c) 0.424%
items.markingKey: (a) 0.00118 mol [1] (b) Rinse apparatus with the solutions; pipette 25.0 cm³ alkali into a conical flask with indicator; add acid from the burette, swirling, dropwise near the end-point; repeat to concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³). [3] (c) two readings: 0.10/23.6 × 100 [1]

items.stem: A beam of neutrons passes between two charged plates. What happens to the beam?
options: It is deflected towards the positive plate
It is deflected towards the negative plate
It is slowed down and stops
items.answer: It is not deflected
items.markingKey: Neutrons are uncharged, so the electric field exerts no force on them.

items.stem: A student in Manila claims that electrons are deflected less than protons because they are smaller. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Electrons are deflected MORE: same size charge but much smaller mass gives a larger charge-to-mass ratio.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: A beam of ³He²⁺ ions is deflected through an angle of 4° when it passes between two charged plates. Calculate the angle through which a beam of ¹H⁺ ions, travelling at the same speed, would be deflected by the same plates.
items.markingKey: angle ∝ charge/mass [1]; ³He²⁺ ions: 2/3, ¹H⁺ ions: 1/1 [1]; angle = 4 × (1/1) ÷ (2/3) = 6.00° [1]

items.stem: A physics–chemistry project in Toronto studies how ions and sub-atomic particles move in an electric field. (a) Copy and complete a table giving the relative mass and relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron. (b) Explain why the electron beam is deflected through a larger angle than the proton beam and in the opposite direction. (c) Predict the effect on the deflection of the proton beam of increasing the voltage across the plates.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) Equal size, opposite charge; much smaller mass (1/1836) so larger charge-to-mass ratio; attracted to the positive plate. (c) Larger deflection, because the electric field and so the force on each proton is greater.
items.markingKey: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 [2] (b) Equal size, opposite charge; much smaller mass (1/1836) so larger charge-to-mass ratio; attracted to the positive plate. [3] (c) Larger deflection, because the electric field and so the force on each proton is greater. [1]

items.stem: Which property differs between ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl?
items.answer: density of the gas
items.markingKey: Physical properties depending on mass (density, rate of diffusion) differ; chemical properties do not.

items.stem: Hana writes in a revision note: "Mg²⁺ is larger than Na⁺ because magnesium has more protons." Identify the error in this statement and give the correct version.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Mg²⁺ is smaller: the ions are isoelectronic and Mg²⁺ has the greater nuclear charge (12 vs 11 protons) pulling the same 10 electrons closer.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the ion ⁴¹K⁺.
items.answer: 19 protons, 22 neutrons, 18 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 19 [1]; neutrons = A − Z = 41 − 19 = 22 [1]; electrons = 19 − (+1) = 18 [1]

items.stem: Use the relative atomic masses in the Periodic Table to find the relative formula mass of CaCO₃.
A sample of bromine from a mineral spring in Dubai contains only ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br. Its relative atomic mass is 79.60. Calculate the percentage abundance of ⁷⁹Br.

A forensic laboratory in Nairobi analyses a sample of chlorine using a mass spectrometer. The peaks are at m/e 35 (abundance 75.8%), m/e 37 (abundance 24.2%). (a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the element to three significant figures. (b) Suggest why a small peak may appear at half of one of the m/e values.
items.answer: (a) 35.5 (b) A doubly charged ion (2+) of that isotope has m/e equal to half its mass.
items.markingKey: (a) Σ(m × %)/100 = 35.5 [2] (b) A doubly charged ion (2+) of that isotope has m/e equal to half its mass. [1]

items.stem: A student in Kathmandu claims that to find the empirical formula you divide each percentage by the atomic number. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Divide each mass (or %) by the relative atomic mass Ar, then by the smallest value.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: Lucas is analysing an unknown compound in an AS practical class. Explain how you would find the formula of a hydrated salt by heating.
items.answer: Weigh, heat to constant mass to remove all water, reweigh; moles of water and anhydrous salt from masses give the ratio x.
items.markingKey: heat to constant mass; calculate mole ratio of water : anhydrous salt [2]

items.stem: A compound has the composition by mass C 69.8%, H 11.6%, O 18.6%. Calculate its empirical formula.
items.answer: C₅H₁₀O
items.markingKey: divide % by Ar [1]; divide by smallest and round to whole numbers: C₅H₁₀O [1]

items.stem: An environmental chemist in Lisbon isolates a pollutant with composition C 54.5%, H 9.1%, O 36.4%. Mass spectrometry shows Mr = 88.0. (a) Define the term empirical formula. (b) Calculate the empirical formula.
items.answer: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. (b) C₂H₄O
items.markingKey: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. [1] (b) divide by Ar, then by smallest, whole-number ratio [2]

items.stem: An environmental chemist in Bogotá isolates a pollutant with composition N 30.4%, O 69.6%. Mass spectrometry shows Mr = 92.0. (a) Define the term empirical formula. (b) Calculate the empirical formula. (c) State the meaning of the term mole.
items.answer: (a) The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. (b) NO₂ (c) The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (as many as there are atoms in 12 g of ¹²C).

items.stem: A chemical company in Dubai uses reacting-mass calculations to plan production. Explain why equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.
items.answer: Gas molecules are far apart, so the volume depends on the number of molecules rather than their size (Avogadro’s law).
items.markingKey: molecules far apart/size negligible; volume depends on number [2]

items.stem: Mateo carries out titrations in an AS practical class. Explain the term limiting reagent.
items.answer: The reactant that is completely used up first; it determines the maximum amount of product, the other reactant being in excess.
items.markingKey: used up first; determines amount of product [2]

items.stem: Elena, a student in Colombo, titrates 25.0 cm³ of 0.0800 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide with sulfuric acid. The mean titre is 19.6 cm³. The equation is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.0510 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Lina uses a standard solution of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid to find the concentration of a solution of sodium hydroxide in a research laboratory. 25.0 cm³ of the alkali needed a mean titre of 22.8 cm³. (a) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. (b) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in mol dm⁻³. (c) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in g dm⁻³.
items.answer: (a) CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O (b) 0.137 mol dm⁻³ (c) 5.47 g dm⁻³
items.markingKey: (a) CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O [1] (b) n(alkali) = 0.00342 mol; ÷ 0.0250 [2] (c) × Mr 40.0 [1]

items.stem: A water-treatment works in Seoul checks the concentration of a sodium carbonate solution by titration with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. A 25.0 cm³ sample needs 21.5 cm³ of acid. (a) Write a balanced equation for the reaction. (b) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in mol dm⁻³. (c) Calculate the concentration of the alkali in g dm⁻³. (d) The burette readings are recorded to the nearest 0.05 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the titre if each reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³.
items.answer: (a) 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ (b) 0.0430 mol dm⁻³ (c) 4.56 g dm⁻³ (d) 0.465%
items.markingKey: (a) 2HCl + Na₂CO₃ → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ [1] (b) n(alkali) = 0.00108 mol; ÷ 0.0250 [2] (c) × Mr 106.0 [1] (d) two readings: 0.10/21.5 × 100 [1]
